member.name: T:Sim.Models.Appendage.FoilAddedMass
member.summary:
Shared computation of a thin foil's hydrodynamic added mass from its wetted geometry, per the Plan B spec (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-29-added-mass-composer-design.md §3). A thin foil's broadside (section-normal) added mass per unit span is the 2-D flat-plate value ρ·π·(c/2)²; integrated over the wetted span (so taper is honoured) and corrected for finite aspect ratio:
A_n = ρ·π·f(AR_eff) · ∫ (chord(s)/2)² ds over the wet sub-span
The hull the foil mounts on acts as a rigid reflection (image) plane, so by the method of images the foil behaves like the inner half of a foil of double span — the effective aspect ratio is doubled: AR_eff = 2·immersedSpan/meanWetChord. f(AR) = AR/(AR+1) is a simple monotonic approximation to flat-plate broadside added-mass-vs-AR data (→1 as AR→∞; for these high-AR foils AR_eff≈8–14 ⇒ f≈0.9–0.95). No free constant — f is computed from the live AR, so retraction lowers both span and AR and added mass falls faster than linearly.
The result is a local diagonal on the section-normal (local-y) axis, (0, A_n, 0); the rotates it into body axes via the appendage's LocalToBody.

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Appendage.ParametricRudderModel
member.summary: Steerable underwater foil (transom-hung rudder) per design-doc §8.3 / §8.6, built on the shared core: station-based NACA , the §15.3 finite-wing polar with section Cl_max / form factor derived per strip from the local thickness ratio, the §21 buoyancy + unified parasitic-drag model, and §20 inertia derived from the planform with an effective density back-solved from the configured mass. Consumes as the blade's rotation about its (raked) stock and returns an carrying StockTorque_Nm for the haptic tiller servo (§18.4).

remarks.para: Sign convention: positive HelmAngle_rad rotates the trailing edge to body +y (port), yawing the bow to port. Positive StockTorque_Nm tends to rotate the rudder further in the +helm direction — the water pushing the rudder the way it's already pointing.

Helm vs. geometry. The cached is helm-free (rake only); chord length is helm-invariant, so helm is applied per tick as the solver's world chord direction, the inertia/added-mass LocalToBody rotation about the raked stock, and (in the renderer) the pintle pivot. Center of pressure (§15.3): the chord-wise CoP starts at CopAftOfStock at α=0 and migrates aft by 0.25·(1−cos α)·chord as |α| grows, so helm load strengthens through stall.

member.name: F:Sim.Models.Environment.IrregularWaveField.DefaultRmsSlopeCap

So every sea a boat could actually be sailing passes, and the guard is what it was designed to be: a net for input no ocean would produce.

member.remarks:
The puff pattern is frozen turbulence (Taylor's hypothesis): a static, seeded 2-D field of Gaussian puffs on a jittered grid, advected as a rigid pattern at DriftFraction × the mean wind. A point at world pos at time t samples the static pattern at pos − drift·t — so a stationary boat still feels puffs sweep past, and a moving boat feels the spatial texture as it crosses it. Every puff's centre, direction swing and speed change is a pure hash of its grid cell, so the whole field is a deterministic, replayable function of (pos, t, seed) with no carried state — safe to sample concurrently across a fleet.
That mean comes from a drift reference the caller supplies, not from the wrapped field, and it must be the un-perturbed base. pos − drift·t is the displacement only while the mean is constant; advecting on an already-shifted mean makes every direction change rewrite the whole elapsed history at once, teleporting the pattern by an amount that grows with t.
Like , it keys off the t handed to , so it sits OUTSIDE a and advances on the sim clock (puffs move in Free Sail / Race, where the environment phase clock is frozen). Only the horizontal wind is perturbed.

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Environment.WeatherClock
member.summary: The clock the moving weather runs on — one instance per world, written once a tick by whoever owns the fleet, read by every boat sampling the wind.

remarks.para: Why weather cannot key off the observer's clock. A wind shift or a puff is a property of the world, not of the boat looking at it: two boats a hull apart must read the same front at the same instant, or they are sailing different weather in one race. But IWindField.Velocity is handed the caller's time, and a caller is a SimSession whose clock is its own step counter. Those counters agree only by convention — every session seeded to the world clock, every boat stepped the same number of times — and a convention is something each new call site has to remember. One that forgets does not fail; it sails a different phase of the shift, which looks like weather.

So the layers read this instead. It is the same move already makes for the base sea and breeze, which samples its inner field at its own regardless of the t it is handed — the difference being that this clock keeps running while that one is frozen, because a pause stops the swell, not the front crossing the course.

A field built without one falls back to the t it is handed. That is the honest answer for a caller with no world — a bench, a solver, the fields' own tests — where the observer's clock is the only clock there is.

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Environment.WindShiftField
member.summary: Wraps an and overlays a superposition of travelling fronts — plane waves in the wind's direction and speed that sweep down the course, the oscillating shift upwind tactics live on. Unlike a time-only oscillation, a front reaches one side of the course before the other, and a boat's encounter rate depends on its heading: beating into the fronts meets them far more often than running away from them.
member.remarks:
The pattern is frozen turbulence (Taylor's hypothesis), the same principle as : a static field of plane waves translated at the base mean wind, so a point at world pos at time t samples the static pattern at pos − U·t. Because U is the un-perturbed base — config-constant during a run — U·t is the exact displacement integral rather than an approximation that rewrites its own history whenever the mean moves.
Each component's front tilt is fixed. A time-varying tilt would make the written phase k(t)·x − ωt diverge from the true ∫(dφ/dt)dt, so the pattern would swing and teleport with error growing as |x|·Δk. Variety comes from the superposition instead: four internally rigid fronts at four tilts sum to a pattern whose apparent line orientation wanders as different components dominate.
Frequency is derived, not configured: expanding kᵢ·(x − U·t) gives ωᵢ = kᵢ·U, so a tilted front sweeps a fixed point more slowly and a moving boat sets its own encounter rate.
Like it keys off the t handed to , so it sits OUTSIDE a and advances on the sim clock (fronts move in Free Sail / Race, where the environment phase clock is frozen).

§15.2 per-face quadratic pressure drag along the face normal. For each wetted face, compute the face-centroid velocity from rigid-body kinematics (v_p = v_cg + ω × (p − p_cg)), project onto the outward normal, and apply F = −½·ρ·Cd·A·|v_n|·v_n · n̂. The sign convention:
v_n < 0 (face moving INTO the water) → force along +n̂ (water pushes back).
v_n > 0 (face moving OUT of the water) → force along −n̂ (symmetric "suction"; physically capped by cavitation but kept symmetric here for stable damping in both directions).
Because the force is applied at the face centroid rather than the CG, lever-arm moments naturally damp rotation as well — this largely subsumes the AngularDrag placeholder once tuned.

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Rig.BendingMast
member.summary:
Dynamic mast bend: a damped modal oscillator per bending plane. The Euler–Bernoulli cantilever (clamped at the deck, free at the masthead, length L = deck→masthead) gives the quasi-static TARGET masthead deflection under the published loads; the served deflection then follows that target through a damped oscillator — mass = , stiffness = the tip stiffness k = 3EI/L³, damping ratio = — integrated quasi-implicitly (stiffness AND damping implicit; closed-form, no iteration, unconditionally stable). This gives the mast real inertia + damping so it can't track the ~22 Hz boom–leech buzz that destabilised the old instantaneous quasi-static mast. One modal DOF (first bending mode); the served shape is q·φ(h). The quasi-static target is additionally amplified by the axial moment-magnifier 1/(1 − P/P_cr) (P-δ): the masthead/leech down-pull compresses the mast and magnifies the transverse bend. The x/y bending planes are linear and decoupled (isotropic EI).
The cantilever is clamped at the deck; the gooseneck rides on the bend at height h_g above the deck. Callers pass heights ABOVE THE GOOSENECK; the mast adds h_g internally before evaluating the cantilever shape/influence.
See spec 2026-06-06-mast-inertia-damping-design.

member.name: P:Sim.Models.Rig.BendingMast.MaxAxialLoadFraction
member.summary:
P-δ axial clamp: the fraction of the Euler buckling load P_cr = π²EI/(4L²) at which the moment-magnifier 1/(1 − P/P_cr) is capped (default 0.3 ⇒ magnifier ≤ 1.43×), so an extreme down-pull can't drive the bend into the buckling singularity. Tuned live.
Lowered from 0.8 (≤ 5×) when the axial height weighting landed. Two reasons, and the first is the real one: this is a static, single-mode magnifier, and a 5× amplification is far outside where such an approximation means anything — past ~1.5 the honest answer is a second-order analysis, not a bigger factor. Second, it is evaluated inside a lagged dynamic loop (the mast reads the sail's shape one tick late), and near the singularity the magnifier's slope is steep enough to turn that lag into a runaway. The old 0.8 only ever survived because the unweighted axial sum let tensile loads low on the mast cancel the masthead's pull; weighting them by height removes that accident.

member.name: M:Sim.Models.Rig.BendingMast.AxialModalWeight(System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary:
The share of a full-column axial load's destabilising effect that a load applied at height actually has. Such a load is reacted at the deck clamp, so it compresses only [0, a]; the work it does against the buckling mode is ∫₀^a φ′²dx as a fraction of ∫₀^L φ′²dx, and φ′ = 3x(2L−x)/(2L³) integrates in closed form. 1.0 at the masthead; **0.0025 at the gooseneck**.
Applied to every axial contribution, the sail's published loads included. Height already governed the transverse path through ; before this the axial path ignored it and charged a load at the gooseneck the same buckling effect as one at the masthead — a factor of ~400. It matters in both directions: MastLoadAssembler publishes a node load at every luff station starting at height 0, and the low ones carry positive (tensile) Z, so weighting them lifts their cancellation of the masthead's pull and P/P_cr goes UP, not down.

member.summary:
XPBD (extended position-based dynamics) solver for the mainsail leech as a chain of point masses between two anchors. Pure dynamics — no sail/aero knowledge. The caller supplies anchors, the per-segment rest lengths (the inextensible leech cloth), per-node chordwise skin caps (a luff point and a max chord), per-node external forces (the leech-corner aero share), node mass, constraint compliances, velocity damping, and the substep schedule. steps the interior nodes one sim step and exposes the new positions plus the per-segment tensions (the edge-constraint multipliers), which the caller feeds to the mast/boom loads.

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Rig.MastLoadAssembler
member.summary: Assembles the distributed 3-D loads the sail puts on the mast, from a per-strip force balance. For each strip i the mast load is the closure F_mast[i] = F_aero[i] + cable@node(i+1), where cable@node(i+1) = T_i·û(node[i+1]→node[i]) + T_{i+1}·û(node[i+1]→node[i+2]) is the same leech force the twist solver already uses. Each contribution is lumped onto the two bracketing luff nodes by its own height, conserving total force and first moment. Only the masthead node touches the mast; interior leech tensions telescope away, leaving Σ loads = Σ F_aero − F_clew (the mast's share). Body frame. The published Force_B is the full 3-D node load: its transverse (X,Y) share bends the mast and its vertical (Z) share is the axial compression a mast model may use for P-δ amplification. See spec 2026-06-06-distributed-mast-load-strip-sail-design.

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Rig.MembraneEdgeSplit
member.summary: Splits a strip's aero resultant into leech-edge and luff-edge reactions via the uniform membrane-tension model (spec 2026-06-09 §6.1). The leech reaction — the edge the leech solver advances — carries the chordwise INWARD pull (T·cosα) that deepens the draft plus its leeward share (T·sinα = N/2); the luff reaction is the remainder F − leech, so the two always sum to the resultant (force-conserving) and the mast load gets its draft-dependent direction without a second edge angle. Below the cloth is too flat to define α (T→∞), so it falls back to today's bilinear chord-normal split (u·F to the leech, (1−u)·F to the luff).

remarks.para: The tension still solves on the virtual (de-roached) leech; only the published corners — aero and render — get the overlay. The roach DISTANCE is read from the cut and never re-derived: the chord only orients the offset, its length dropped by the normalize. The overlay is rigid, so it reproduces the real chord in the design pose and approximates it as the leech stretches.

Which is why it is derived, and why the wire carries the virtual leech. Every input is the solved nodes, the luff and the static cut, so a client holding those calls this and gets the solver's own corners — and feeds the VIRTUAL nodes it was sent to , which is the leech that call has always wanted. Publishing the roachy corners instead left a client with a chord ~12% long on the ILCA cut and a reconstructed draft of exactly zero.

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Util.FoilPolar
member.summary: Finite-wing foil polar (lift & induced-drag coefficients vs. angle of attack) shared by all hydrodynamic-lifting-surface models — keel/daggerboard, rudder, and any future foils. Replaces the AR-independent Cl = Cl_max·sin(2α) placeholder previously inlined in ParametricKeelModel / ParametricRudderModel.

remarks.para: Pre-stall (|α| ≤ α_stall): linear lifting-line theory. Cl = a_3D · α with finite-wing slope a_3D = 2π·AR/(AR+2) (per radian). Induced drag is lift-coupled: Cd_i = Cl² / (π·AR·e) where e is the Oswald span efficiency (typical 0.75–0.95).

Post-stall / reverse (|α| > α_stall): inviscid flat-plate Cl = Cl_max·sin(2α), peaking at Cl_max at 45°, tapering to zero at 90°, and continued symmetrically into the reverse half (sign-flipping). There is a downward step at the stall angle (Cl_max → Cl_max·sin(2α_stall)) — the physical stall drop; the model is intentionally not C1- or C0-continuous there. Normal-force form drag Cd_form = Cd_n90·t² tents about broadside via t = (δ−α_stall)/(π/2−α_stall) with δ = min(|α|, π−|α|), so it peaks at α=90° and returns to zero as the flow re-aligns from behind. The stall flag covers the separated mid-band α_stall < |α| < π−α_stall only.

Fore-aft symmetry (modeling simplification). The post-stall lift is continued symmetrically across the full angle range, so the section is treated as fore-aft symmetric: reverse-flow lift (|α| > 90°, flow over the trailing edge) has the same magnitude as forward-flow lift at the supplementary angle. A real foil is not fore-aft symmetric — its rounded leading edge and sharp trailing edge mean that in reverse the sharp edge leads, tripping earlier separation, so a real keel/rudder makes less lift and more drag backing up than going forward. We deliberately omit this: reverse is low-speed maneuvering where forces (∝ V²) are small, and the lift direction — the thing that makes reverse steering work — is already correct. If higher reverse fidelity is ever needed, attenuate the reverse half with a per-foil ReverseLiftEfficiency factor; it can be applied as a step at α=90° without a discontinuity, since Cl=0 there. (The center-of-pressure migration, by contrast, IS quadrant-aware — see — and is not waived by this simplification.)

Center of pressure migrates aft from the aerodynamic center (c/4) at α=0, through the centroid (c/2) at broadside (α=±90°), and on toward c·¾ in full reverse (α=±180°) — modeled by as a quadrant-aware 0.25·(1−cos α) shift aft of the static offset (so absolute x_CoP/c = 0.5 − 0.25·cos α for a quarter-chord static CoP). Used by the rudder model to give a physically-correct stock-torque feel that strengthens through stall and keeps migrating aft when the flow reverses.

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Util.HydroStrip
member.summary: Pure, stateless per-strip hydrodynamics for a lifting surface (§15.3). Given a resolved inflow and the strip's own leading/trailing-edge points (plus span direction, width, section thickness, and the whole-foil wet aspect ratio), it returns the strip's force, application point (centre of pressure), and force components. It knows nothing of waves, rigid-body state, or how the foil is placed — the caller () resolves all of that and hands each strip its local inflow and edge geometry. This is what makes the per-strip physics unit-testable without standing up a boat, and turns the whole-foil check into a force summation over strips.
member.remarks: The centre of pressure is read straight from the geometry: CoP = LE + (StaticCopFraction + migration(α)) · (TE − LE), so it honours taper/sweep and migrates aft with angle of attack. StaticCopFraction is the static chord-wise baseline as a fraction of the local chord (¼-chord aerodynamic centre for a normal foil); the caller supplies it.

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Util.LiftingSurfaceGeometry
member.summary: Strip / panel kinematics for a lifting surface, in the chord-span-normal section plane. Pure geometry — no density, no polar, no force magnitudes. Consumed by both (water foils: keel, rudder) and the panel-discretised mainsail model (air) so the heel / cant / twist projection is implemented in one place and stays consistent.
member.remarks: For a surface with span direction s and chord direction c in world frame, only the inflow component perpendicular to s produces lift (infinite-yawed-wing approximation). α is measured in the plane perpendicular to s, between the chord's own in-plane projection and the projected inflow; the lift vector is unit-normal to the projected inflow within that plane. Skin friction and any pressure-drag terms that act on the real surface velocity stay outside this kernel — the caller handles those with the full inflow.

member.name: M:Sim.Models.Util.NacaSection.FormFactor(System.Single)
member.summary: Pressure-drag form factor k in the (1 + k) multiplier on skin friction (). Hoerner's streamlined-section correlation: k = 2·(t/c) + 60·(t/c)⁴. At t/c = 0.09 this gives ≈ 0.184; at 0.12, ≈ 0.252 — both inside the 0.10–0.25 band the models used to hardcode at 0.15.

member.name: M:Sim.Models.Util.NacaSection.SectionClMax(System.Single)
member.summary: Section (2-D) maximum lift coefficient vs. thickness ratio, which sets stall onset in (α_stall = Cl_max / a_3D(AR)) and the post-stall amplitude. Thin sections stall early and low; lift rises with thickness to a peak near ~15 % then rolls off. Capped quadratic anchored at the foils' operating Reynolds (~3–6e5, NOT the 3–6e6 wind- tunnel maxima, where Cl_max is ~15–20 % higher): NACA 0006 ≈ 0.85, 0009 ≈ 1.07, 0012 ≈ 1.20, 0015 ≈ 1.24 (peak), 0018 ≈ 1.20. Clamped to [0.6, 1.5]. (A daggerboard at Re≈5e5 makes noticeably less peak lift than the same section in a high-Re tunnel; using the tunnel maxima over-predicts post-stall side force.)

member.name: T:Sim.Models.Util.WaveMakingDrag
member.summary: Parametric wave-making (residuary) resistance, per design-doc §15.2 and the 2026-06-08 hull-wave-drag spec. Wave-making drag is a non-local, Froude-driven effect (energy radiated into surface gravity waves) with no cheap per-face form, so it is modelled as a scalar Cw(Fr) curve applied along the hull's forward axis. All knobs are feel-tuned in the live sim; this helper owns only the math.

member.name: M:Sim.Models.Util.WaveMakingDrag.Cw(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Asymmetric-Gaussian residuary-resistance coefficient: near-zero at low Fr, peaking at (≈ hull speed), then decaying as the boat climbs onto plane. Separate rise/fall widths (/) shape the "wall" and how cleanly the boat lets go onto plane. The low-Fr tail of the Gaussian keeps Cw ≈ 0 below ~0.2 for the default widths (no hard cutoff → no discontinuity).
